For a $T$-query quantum algorithm [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]] at input length $n$, its **worst-case quantum query cost** is the maximum number of designated oracle calls over all promised instances in $P_n$ and all measurement branches. When $P_n$ is empty, define this cost to be $0$. For nonempty $P_n$, a finite circuit and finite branch sets ensure that this maximum exists; a solver whose branch counts are not uniformly bounded has infinite worst-case query cost. An expected-query bound is the separate quantity defined by [[def-qa-expected-query-cost]].

citations.quote: Fix an integer $n\ge0$, put $N=2^n$, and let $D_n=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$. The big-endian encoding $\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to D_n$ is a bijection by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]], so identify each address word $w$ with its slot $x=\operatorname{enc}_n(w)$. A search instance is a total Boolean function $f:D_n\to\{0,1\}$, equivalently the word-indexed function $w\mapsto f(\operatorname{enc}_n(w))$. Its marked set is $M=\{x\in D_n:f(x)=1\}$ and its marked count is $t=|M|$. The standard bit query is the coherent XOR action $U_f|x,b\rangle=|x,b\oplus f(x)\rangle$; the associated phase query is $O_M|x\rangle=(-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle$. One standard bit query implements this phase action with a response qubit prepared in $|-\rangle$, by [[thm-qa-bit-query-to-phase-query]]. A measured candidate $x$ is verified by a separate standard bit query. Knowing $t$ is additional classical input; no count promise is made in the unknown-count version. A correct search output is a verified $x\in M$. The distinguished output none is used only by a procedure whose input includes the exact fact $t=0$; it is not a finite-time test for emptiness when $t$ is unknown.

derivations.claim: Let $|s\rangle=N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|j\rangle$, $P_s=|s\rangle\langle s|$, and let the fixed marked coordinate be $i$. Its query address is $i-1$, so the phase query $O_i=I-2|i-1\rangle\langle i-1|$ sends $s$ to the unit vector $\psi_i=s-2|i-1\rangle/\sqrt N$ because it only flips one basis sign; set $P_{\psi_i}=|\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$. Orthonormality [F2] gives $\langle s,\psi_i\rangle_D=1-2/N$; [F5]–[F6] give $D(P_s,P_{\psi_i})=\sqrt{1-(1-2/N)^2}=2\sqrt{N-1}/N=O(N^{-1/2})$. This tends to zero with $N$.

Suppose instead the mark is unknown and uniform on $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Each $P_{\psi_i}$ is a density operator by [F4], so their finite average $\rho=N^{-1}\sum_iP_{\psi_i}$ is self-adjoint, nonnegative, and trace one. Writing $e_i=|i-1\rangle$, expansion gives $P_{\psi_i}=P_s-\frac2{\sqrt N}(|s\rangle\langle e_i|+|e_i\rangle\langle s|)+\frac4N|e_i\rangle\langle e_i|$. The two cross sums each equal $\sqrt N P_s$, and $\sum_i|e_i\rangle\langle e_i|=I$ by [F2]–[F3], so $\rho=(1-4/N)P_s+4I/N^2$. Then $X=\rho-P_s$ has eigenvalue $-4(N-1)/N^2$ on $\operatorname{span}\{s\}$ and $4/N^2$ on $s^\perp$ of dimension $N-1$; their sum with multiplicity is zero, so $X$ is trace-zero. Its negative part is $X_-=(4(N-1)/N^2)P_s$, whose trace is $4(N-1)/N^2$ because $P_s$ has trace one. By [F5] and [F7], $D(\rho,P_s)=\tfrac12\|X\|_1=4(N-1)/N^2=O(N^{-1})$. If $N=1$, $s^\perp$ has dimension zero and the formula gives distance zero.

By [F8], any measurement on either post-query state changes its outcome law from the initial uniform state's law by at most the corresponding trace distance in steps 1.1 and 1.2. Both distances tend to zero with $N$, so neither specified experiment has constant measurement advantage for large $N$. The lower bound [F9] concerns arbitrary algorithms and is proved independently; it is not inferred from this example.
